title: Curd vs Paneer: Which Actually Has More Protein?
meta_description: 100g paneer has 18-20g protein at 265-295 kcal. Plain dahi has only 3-4g protein per 100g — Greek yogurt closes that gap to 9-11g, but usually at 4-5x the cost per gram of protein. Here's how to actually use each one.
meta_keywords: curd vs paneer protein, dahi protein content, greek yogurt vs paneer, hung curd protein, paneer vs curd weight loss
quick_answer: Paneer wins on protein density by a wide margin: 18-20g protein per 100g versus about 3-4g in plain dahi. Greek yogurt narrows the gap to roughly 9-11g protein per 100g, but it's usually priced at four to five times what plain dahi costs per gram of protein. The two aren't really competing for the same job — paneer is a calorie-dense protein source for a main meal, while dahi is a light, low-calorie addition better valued for digestion and volume than for hitting protein numbers.

faq.question: Does curd (dahi) have enough protein to count as a protein source?
faq.answer: Plain full-fat dahi has about 3-4g protein per 100g — roughly the same as the milk it's made from, since fermentation doesn't add protein. A typical 200g bowl gives you 6-8g protein, which is worth counting but won't move the needle the way paneer, eggs, or dal will. Treat dahi as a supporting source, not a primary one.

faq.question: Is Greek yogurt a better protein source than paneer in India?
faq.answer: Not by protein-per-rupee. Greek yogurt typically has 9-11g protein per 100g versus paneer's 18-20g, so you need roughly twice the weight of Greek yogurt to match paneer's protein. Combined with Greek yogurt's premium pricing in Indian supermarkets, it usually costs four to five times more per gram of protein than paneer. It's a reasonable snack or breakfast option, but not a cost-efficient way to hit a protein target.

faq.question: Is hung curd a good middle ground between dahi and paneer?
faq.answer: Yes, for protein density. Straining plain dahi through muslin cloth to drain the whey (making hung curd or chakka) concentrates the protein to roughly 6-8g per 100g, since some of the water weight is removed while the protein stays behind. It's a useful base for dips, spreads, or a thicker breakfast bowl — though it's still well short of paneer's density.

intro: Dahi and paneer sit next to each other in most Indian fridges, and both get called out as "good protein" in general health advice. They're not in the same league, and treating them as interchangeable leads to bad math — someone counting on a bowl of curd to match a paneer sabzi is going to fall short by a lot. Here's what each one actually delivers, including where Greek yogurt fits and where it doesn't.

sections.heading: The numbers, side by side
sections.body:
Per 100g:

• Plain full-fat dahi (whole milk curd): 3-4g protein, 60-65 kcal
• Low-fat dahi (skimmed milk curd): 3.5-4g protein, 40-55 kcal
• Hung curd / chakka (dahi strained of whey): 6-8g protein, 90-110 kcal
• Greek yogurt (commercial, strained-style): 9-11g protein, 55-65 kcal
• Full-fat paneer: 18-20g protein, 265-295 kcal

Paneer has roughly five times the protein density of plain dahi and nearly double that of Greek yogurt. It's also far more calorie-dense, which is the trade-off: you get more protein per 100g, but you also get more calories per 100g.

sections.heading: Why dahi's protein number is so low
sections.body:
Curd is just fermented milk, and fermentation doesn't add protein — the culture converts lactose to lactic acid, which is what gives dahi its tang and thickness, but the protein content stays close to whatever the starting milk had. Standard Indian dairy milk runs about 3-3.5g protein per 100ml, and dahi made from it lands in the same range.

This is why a 200g bowl of dahi — a generous serving — gives you only 6-8g protein, less than a single egg. It's a fine addition to a meal for gut health, cooling effect, and volume, but it was never going to be a serious protein contributor on its own.

sections.heading: Greek yogurt: real protein bump, real price bump
sections.body:
Commercial Greek-style yogurt (Epigamia, Nestlé a2, and similar brands sold in India) genuinely does concentrate more protein than regular dahi — typically 9-11g per 100g, achieved by straining out extra whey during production, similar in principle to hung curd but more thoroughly done.

The catch is price. Plain dahi typically costs ₹60-90/kg, working out to roughly ₹1.9-2.6 per gram of protein. Greek yogurt in India is usually sold in small cups at a steep per-kg markup — often ₹400-550/kg equivalent — putting the cost at roughly ₹4-5.5 per gram of protein, noticeably more than paneer's ₹1.9-2.2 per gram (using the ₹350-400/kg range typical for branded paneer). Greek yogurt is a genuinely higher-protein food than plain dahi, but it isn't a cost-efficient one next to paneer or plain dal.

sections.heading: Hung curd: a reasonable middle option
sections.body:
Straining plain dahi through muslin cloth for a few hours drains off the watery whey and leaves a thicker, more concentrated curd — commonly called hung curd or chakka. Because whey carries some protein away with it but proportionally less than the water it's dissolved in, the remaining curd ends up somewhat more protein-dense, typically 6-8g per 100g against the original 3-4g.

It's a genuinely useful kitchen trick: hung curd works as a base for raita, dips, or a thicker breakfast bowl with fruit, and it's essentially free to make from dahi you already have. It won't replace paneer for protein, but it's a real, no-cost step up from plain dahi.

sections.heading: Which one should actually be on your plate
sections.body:
These two foods aren't really solving the same problem, so "which is better" depends on what you need from the meal:

• If you need protein density for a main dish — a sabzi, tikka, or bhurji-style preparation — paneer is the clear choice at 18-20g per 100g.

• If you want a light, cooling, low-calorie side that helps digestion and adds volume to a meal without much calorie cost, plain dahi does that job well — just don't count on it for protein.

• If you want something in between — more protein than dahi, less commitment than paneer, and useful for dips or a thicker breakfast — hung curd or Greek yogurt both work, with hung curd being the more budget-friendly of the two.

A day that uses paneer at one meal and dahi as a side at another, rather than picking one over the other, gets the benefit of both without over-relying on either.

key_takeaways: 100g paneer has 18-20g protein versus just 3-4g in plain dahi — roughly a 5x difference
Fermentation doesn't add protein to milk, which is why dahi's protein content mirrors the milk it's made from
Greek yogurt raises protein to 9-11g per 100g but typically costs 4-5x more per gram of protein than paneer
Hung curd (strained dahi) is a free, easy way to concentrate protein to roughly 6-8g per 100g
Paneer and dahi solve different problems — use paneer for protein density, dahi for a light, gut-friendly side
